issues.legal_issue: An acquisition for a company cannot be invalidated for non-compliance with mandatory acquisition procedures on a bare, unparticularised allegation when the record demonstrates compliance.
material_facts: The challenges alleged non-compliance with the company-acquisition rules, but did not give particulars showing how the rules had been breached; in one challenge, there was no allegation concerning the committee requirement at all.

The State and the acquiring company produced affidavits and documents showing that the committee had been constituted and consulted and that the prescribed inquiry and other requirements had been carried out.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to set aside the acquisition on the ground that the company-acquisition rules had not been complied with.
issues.legal_principle: Rules 3 and 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 are mandatory. A party alleging breach of a statutory requirement must plead particulars sufficient to establish an issue; a bare allegation ordinarily warrants no action. The Court also held that a Collector may obtain and act on an Assistant Collector’s report and need not personally examine every detail.

predicates.company_land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges an acquisition undertaken for a company.
predicates.specific_breach_particulars_absent: The challenger does not set out facts specifying how the required acquisition procedures were breached.
predicates.official_records_show_compliance: The government record and supporting evidence show that the required procedures were followed.

issues.definition: When a company-acquisition challenge lacks particulars of the alleged procedural breach and the record shows compliance, the challenge fails on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: Acquisition proceedings are not invalid for failure to serve compensation-inquiry notices when the challengers admit that the notices were served.
material_facts: The challengers’ own writ petition stated that they had received separate notices requiring them to appear in connection with the acquisition.
They stated that they made a representation to the acquisition officers after receiving those notices.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to find that the challengers had not been served with the notices.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for notice to interested persons to state their interests and compensation claims. On the admitted facts, the Court found that notice had been served; it did not decide the separate question whether service was legally required in the circumstances.

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenges a land acquisition on the ground that required notices were not served.
predicates.challengers_admit_notice_service: The challengers themselves acknowledge that they received the notices.

issues.definition: When challengers acknowledge receiving the notices, their challenge cannot succeed on the claim that those notices were not served.

issues.legal_issue: A witnessed possession memorandum, considered with the surrounding official records and circumstances, can establish that possession of acquired open land was taken and delivered.
material_facts: A possession memorandum recorded that an officer took possession of open land in the presence of two witnesses and delivered it to the acquiring company’s representative.
The memorandum was signed by the officers involved, and a possession receipt was also signed.
The revenue records showed the acquiring company as being in possession; the land had no construction or crops when possession was taken.
The challengers later filed witness affidavits contradicting the memorandum, but the Court found them unpersuasive.
issues.conclusion: Possession had been taken and delivered; the High Court was wrong to find otherwise.
issues.legal_principle: In Balwant Narayan Bhagde v. M.D. Bhagwat, the Court explained that taking possession depends on the nature of the land and that the owner’s presence is not essential. Tamil Nadu Housing Board v. Viswam and Balmokand Khatri Educational and Industrial Trust v. State of Punjab recognise a witnessed panchnama or possession memorandum as an accepted mode of taking possession; continued occupation thereafter may be unlawful possession. The Court cautioned that a High Court should not disregard the memorandum and revenue record on the basis of contradictory affidavits.

predicates.acquired_land_possession_dispute: The parties dispute whether possession of land acquired by the government was taken.
predicates.witnessed_possession_record_exists: An official memorandum records the taking of possession in the presence of witnesses.
predicates.official_records_support_transfer: Other official records support that possession was transferred to the acquiring body.

issues.definition: In a dispute over possession of acquired land, a witnessed official record supported by other official records establishes that possession was taken.

issues.legal_issue: A writ challenge to acquisition notifications may be barred by laches when the challenger waits until the acquisition has proceeded to completion despite grounds for challenge being available earlier.
material_facts: The acquisition notifications and declaration were issued before the challengers filed their writ petition.
The challengers filed the petition only after notices had issued and possession had been taken, although the grounds they raised were available earlier.
issues.conclusion: The challenge was barred by laches as well as failing on its other grounds.
issues.legal_principle: The Court reiterated that a challenge to acquisition notifications must be brought within a reasonable time. A person cannot wait while the government completes acquisition proceedings on the basis that the notifications are valid and then raise grounds that were already available, since that would reward delay.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification_challenge: A party brings a writ challenge to notifications or a declaration initiating or advancing a land acquisition.
predicates.challenge_brought_after_proceedings_adva: The challenger waits until the acquisition has substantially proceeded before filing the challenge.
predicates.grounds_available_earlier: The grounds relied on were available to the challenger before the acquisition substantially proceeded.

issues.definition: A challenge to acquisition notifications is barred by laches when it is brought only after proceedings have substantially advanced on grounds that were available earlier.

issues.legal_issue: Withdrawal from acquisition under the statutory withdrawal power must be notified in the Official Gazette.
material_facts: The State Government decided to withdraw land from acquisition by issuing internal memoranda and communicated those decisions to the acquiring company.
No withdrawal notification had been published in the Official Gazette.
issues.conclusion: Withdrawal from acquisition requires publication of a notification in the Official Gazette; an internal decision or memorandum alone does not effect the withdrawal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for withdrawal from acquisition and for compensation for damage caused by acquisition proceedings. Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 concerns the power to rescind instruments issued under statutory authority. The Court held that, once notifications under Sections 4 and 6 have advanced the acquisition process, withdrawal under Section 48 must be notified; rescinding the earlier notifications alone is insufficient. It relied on State of Maharashtra v. Umashankar Rajabhau, U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties, and Murari v. Union of India.

predicates.statutory_acquisition_withdrawal: The government decides to withdraw land from an acquisition governed by a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.acquisition_notifications_already_issued: Formal notifications initiating or declaring the acquisition have already been issued.

issues.definition: When the government withdraws land after formal acquisition notifications have issued, the withdrawal takes effect only through publication in the Official Gazette.

issues.legal_issue: The government may withdraw land from acquisition only before possession has been taken.
material_facts: The acquiring company had been put in possession of part of the land under a witnessed possession memorandum.
The State Government later decided to withdraw that land from acquisition.
issues.conclusion: Withdrawal from acquisition was impermissible to the extent that possession had already been taken.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 permits withdrawal from acquisition where possession of the land has not been taken. The Court relied on U.P. Jal Nigam v. Kalra Properties for the principle that, once possession has been taken and the land has vested in the State, it cannot be divested except through a valid withdrawal under Section 48 before possession is taken.

predicates.statutory_acquisition_withdrawal: The government decides to withdraw land from an acquisition governed by a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.possession_already_taken: The government or acquiring body has already taken possession of the land.

issues.definition: The government cannot withdraw land from acquisition after possession of that land has been taken.

issues.legal_issue: A landowner whose land is withdrawn from acquisition need not be given prior notice of the proposed withdrawal, because the statutory compensation provisions protect the owner against resulting damage.
material_facts: The State Government decided to withdraw land from acquisition following applications by landowners who said that acquisition had caused them hardship.
The acquiring company, rather than the landowners, challenged the withdrawal decisions.
issues.conclusion: A landowner need not be given notice of the State Government’s intention to withdraw; any damage suffered by the owner in consequence of the acquisition proceedings is addressed through the statutory compensation provisions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provides for compensation for damage suffered in consequence of acquisition proceedings, and Section 48(3) provides for determination of that compensation. The Court distinguished the position of a landowner, whose interests are protected by those provisions, from that of a company for whose benefit land is being acquired.

predicates.statutory_acquisition_withdrawal: The government decides to withdraw land from an acquisition governed by a statutory acquisition process.
predicates.affected_person_is_landowner: The person whose interests are affected by the withdrawal is the owner of the land being released from acquisition.

issues.definition: When the affected person is the landowner, withdrawal from acquisition does not require a prior hearing for that owner.

issues.legal_issue: A company for whose benefit acquisition proceedings have reached the statutory consent and agreement stages must be given an opportunity to oppose the government’s proposed withdrawal.
material_facts: The land was proposed to be acquired for the company’s housing colony after the required inquiries and company-acquisition procedures had been completed.
The State Government decided to withdraw some of the land without giving the company notice or an opportunity to respond.
The company asserted that the released land was needed for its housing scheme and that its release would prejudice the scheme.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal decisions were unlawful because the company had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed withdrawal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 39–42 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require prior government consent, an inquiry, an agreement with the company, and publication of the agreement in the Official Gazette for an acquisition for a company. Rules 3 and 4 of the Land Acquisition (Companies) Rules, 1963 provide for a committee and an inquiry into specified matters. Once these requirements have been completed and a Section 6 declaration is made, a valuable right accrues to the company to oppose proposed withdrawal. In Amarnath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of Uttar Pradesh, the Court distinguished the company beneficiary’s position from that of a landowner and recognised the possibility of substantial prejudice to the company.

rule.if: company_beneficiary_acquisition and company_acquisition_procedures_completed and proposed_withdrawal_may_prejudice_company and company_given_no_opportunity_to_respond

predicates.company_beneficiary_acquisition: The acquisition is being undertaken for the benefit of a company.
predicates.company_acquisition_procedures_completed: The statutory procedures applicable to acquiring land for a company have been completed.
predicates.proposed_withdrawal_may_prejudice_compan: The proposed release of the land may adversely affect the company’s intended use or plans for the acquisition.
predicates.company_given_no_opportunity_to_respond: The government makes its withdrawal decision without giving the company an opportunity to oppose it.

issues.definition: When company-acquisition procedures are complete and a proposed withdrawal may prejudice the beneficiary company, a withdrawal made without giving the company an opportunity to respond is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The government’s discretion to withdraw from acquisition is reviewable and cannot be exercised arbitrarily or in bad faith when the withdrawal may prejudice a company beneficiary.
material_facts: The company challenged the State Government’s decisions to release land acquired for its housing scheme.
The State relied on landowners’ applications and asserted that it had verified their claims before deciding to release the land.
The Court held that the company’s interests could be substantially prejudiced by withdrawal, while resolving the challenge on the ground that the company had not been given an opportunity to respond.
issues.conclusion: The State Government’s discretion to withdraw is not absolute or immune from judicial review; a withdrawal may be challenged if the power was exercised mala fide or arbitrarily.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 confers discretion to withdraw, but does not authorise arbitrary action. The Court relied on Amarnath Ashram Trust Society v. Governor of Uttar Pradesh for the distinction between an owner’s challenge and a beneficiary company’s challenge, and on Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Godrej & Boyce while explaining that the latter decision did not make the government’s discretion unreviewable in every case.

predicates.company_beneficiary_challenges_withdrawa: A company for whose benefit land was acquired challenges the government’s decision to withdraw from the acquisition.
predicates.withdrawal_may_prejudice_company: The withdrawal may substantially adversely affect the company’s interests.
predicates.withdrawal_is_arbitrary_or_mala_fide: The government’s exercise of its withdrawal power is arbitrary or made in bad faith.

issues.definition: When a company beneficiary faces possible prejudice from a withdrawal, an arbitrary or bad-faith decision may be invalidated.
